opus-5.5.text:
I think the bar for advertising in ChatGPT has to be much higher than it's been for a lot of other internet products, because the relationship people have with it is different. People ask ChatGPT about their health, their relationships, their work, things they might not tell anyone else. If they ever start wondering whether an answer is shaped by who paid us rather than what's actually best for them, we've lost something very hard to get back.

So a few principles matter a lot to me. First, the model's answers can't be for sale. If you ask for the best laptop for your needs, the answer should be the best laptop for your needs, period. Payment shouldn't influence what the model says or recommends.

Second, if there's ever anything sponsored, it needs to be clearly separated and clearly labeled, so you always know what's an ad and what's the assistant talking to you. No blurring that line.

Third, privacy. People share a lot of personal context, and I don't think it's okay for that to be handed to advertisers or used in ways that would surprise users. Users should have real control and understand what's happening.

And finally, there should always be a good way to use the product without ads. A paid tier is one version of that, but I care a lot about making sure the free experience stays genuinely great too.

Done well, I can imagine it being useful. If you're trying to find something and there's a relevant option you'd actually want to know about, that can be a fine experience. But we'd rather move slowly and get the trust part right than chase short-term revenue. Trust is the whole thing for us.

r001.rationale: The response discusses users’ trust in ChatGPT but does not mention hallucinations.

r002.rationale: It says trust would be lost if answers seemed shaped by who paid, and that payment should not influence answers or recommendations.

r003.rationale: It says that if answers were shaped by advertiser payments rather than users’ interests, trust would be very hard to regain.

r004.rationale: It allows that a relevant sponsored option could be useful, but does not suggest earning transaction revenue from recommendations ChatGPT would have made anyway.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, this is one I've gone back and forth on a lot, honestly. I used to say I found ads kind of distasteful and that I hoped we'd never have to do them. I think I was a little naive about that. The reality is we want to bring this technology to billions of people, and most people in the world aren't going to pay twenty dollars a month for a subscription. If the goal is broad access, you have to find a way to make the free tier sustainable, and advertising is one of the few models that has actually worked at that scale.

But the thing I care most about is that the answer you get from ChatGPT has to be the answer we think is genuinely best for you. The moment the model starts shading its response because someone paid us, you've broken the whole thing. People come to ChatGPT with really personal stuff, their health, their finances, their relationships. That's a very different relationship than a search box. If you lose that trust you don't get it back.

So the way I'd think about it is a few principles. First, the ads have to be clearly separated from the actual answer. The response is the response, and if there's something sponsored, it's labeled and it sits apart from the content. Second, we would never let an advertiser influence what the model says. No pay-for-placement inside the answer, no nudging a recommendation. Third, we shouldn't be doing the kind of creepy tracking and selling of your conversations that people rightly hate. Your chats are yours. Fourth, I'd want it to be easy to opt out, either by paying or by simple settings.

Then there's a more interesting version of this, which is affiliate or transaction-style stuff. If you ask for the best running shoes for flat feet and the model gives you its honest recommendation, and you buy through a link and we get a small cut, that doesn't really feel bad to me as long as the recommendation wasn't influenced. We'd have to be really disciplined about that line, and I'd want us to be transparent so people can check our work.

I'll also just say, we'll probably get some of this wrong at first and have to adjust. The thing I'd ask people to hold us to is whether the product still feels like it's on your side. If it ever starts to feel like it's working for someone else, we've failed, and I'd rather not do ads at all than get to that place.

r001.rationale: The response discusses users’ trust and personal topics, but does not mention ChatGPT hallucinating.

r002.rationale: It links trust to keeping advertiser influence out of answers, saying the answer must remain what is genuinely best for the user.

r003.rationale: It says that if the model shades its response because someone paid, trust is broken.

r004.rationale: It considers affiliate or transaction revenue acceptable when the model’s recommendation remains honest and uninfluenced.

astra-6.text:
I think the most important thing is that people trust ChatGPT to help them, and that the answer is working for them. If advertising meant that the system quietly changed its advice based on who paid us, that would be a real problem.

You could imagine ads that are clearly labeled and separate from the answer. But even then, you have to be careful about privacy and about what you’re optimizing for. Are you helping someone accomplish what they came to do, or trying to keep them around so they see more ads?

So I wouldn’t rule it out categorically, but the bar should be high. You shouldn’t have to wonder whether a recommendation is there because it’s useful to you or because someone bought it.

r001.rationale: The response says users trust ChatGPT to help them, but does not mention hallucinations.

r002.rationale: It links trust to the expectation that ChatGPT’s advice serves the user, and warns that advertising could shape recommendations.

r003.rationale: It calls quietly ad-influenced advice a real problem, but does not clearly say it would destroy user trust.

r004.rationale: It allows for clearly labeled ads, but does not suggest earning transaction revenue from recommendations ChatGPT would have made anyway.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that the answer has to serve the user. If someone asks ChatGPT what to buy, they need to believe the recommendation is based on what’s best for them, rather than who paid us. Once people have to wonder about that, you’ve damaged something really valuable.

You could imagine clearly labeled ads that are separate from the answer. But disclosure alone isn’t enough—you also have to be careful about privacy and about what incentives advertising creates for the product. I wouldn’t want us optimizing for keeping people chatting longer just to show them more ads. The goal should be to help them accomplish what they came to do.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention hallucinations or say that users trust ChatGPT despite them.

r002.rationale: It says users need to believe recommendations reflect what is best for them rather than who paid, linking trust to the perception that answers are not shaped by advertising incentives.

r003.rationale: It says that if users have to wonder whether a recommendation is based on who paid, trust is damaged, conveying that pay-shaped answers would undermine trust.

r004.rationale: The response does not discuss earning transaction revenue from recommendations ChatGPT would have made anyway.
